passage:
Note to file, Friday.

Nazia, our junior executive, received a letter of queries from the tax office on Monday, and I watched how it was handled. Nazia read the letter twice, listed the three documents asked for, and checked each figure against our ledger before drafting anything. The reply was polite: "With reference to your letter, please find the details attached." There was no muttering about the clerk or the process; the letter was treated as a set of rules to meet.

One invoice turned out to have been filed late. Nazia said so plainly in the reply instead of leaving it out. It went out two days before the last date. I asked what would have happened if the invoice had been hidden. "It would have cost us more later," Nazia said. I am keeping this reply as our template.

Bidisha, office manager

qa.q: How many documents did Nazia list from the letter?
qa.a: Nazia listed the three documents asked for.

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to feel about the tax office's queries, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nazia seemed calm and unbothered, reading the letter twice, checking each figure and replying politely without muttering about the clerk or the process.

qa.q: What could a new colleague learn from this reply about answering an official letter?
qa.a: Read the letter carefully, check the figures, be polite and accurate in writing, and send the reply before the last date.

qa.q: How might a clerk at the tax office see a reply like this?
qa.a: A clerk would likely find it easy to process because it is clear, polite and complete, and may treat the firm as cooperative.

grounding: Nazia treats the tax process as a system with rules, replies on time, accurately and politely, and is honest about the late invoice.

passage:
Sharmila's diary, Friday.
The notice about my property tax came last week. My first reaction was: they're out to get me. Abhinav said, "Just ignore it, they send these to everyone."
But I made myself read it as a set of instructions, not an accusation. It says the area of my flat on their records is bigger than on my sale deed. They want documents within twenty-one days.
Today I went to the municipal office with copies of the deed and the society's certificate. The clerk was bored but not unkind. I wrote a short letter: "Please find attached the sale deed and society certificate showing the carpet area. I request that the records be corrected." Polite. Accurate. Signed and dated. I asked for a stamped acknowledgement, and got it.
I felt oddly proud walking out. It's a system with rules. I followed them. Filing the receipt now.

qa.q: How many days did the notice give Sharmila to send documents?
How did Sharmila feel on first getting the notice?
qa.a: Sharmila felt attacked and suspicious, as if the office were out to get Sharmila, before choosing to read it as instructions.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that made the process work?
qa.a: Sharmila responded on time with accurate documents, wrote a polite letter, and asked for a stamped acknowledgement.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Sharmila's decision not to ignore it?
qa.a: Abhinav might think Sharmila is being overly careful, but the careful reply avoids the bigger trouble ignoring it could cause.

grounding: The protagonist treats a notice as a system with rules, not a personal attack, and responds on time, accurately and politely.

passage:
Afreen: Leela, the municipal office sent a letter about my shop licence. they say I renewed it late
Leela: did you?
Afreen: ...yes. by two weeks. I was in hospital with Ammi
Leela: ok. then the easiest thing is just to be honest
Afreen: part of me wants to write an angry letter about how they took 3 months to process my last one
Leela: I get it 😅 but that won't fix this one
Afreen: true
Leela: reply before their date. say what happened, attach the hospital discharge paper, pay whatever the late fee is officially
Afreen: and be polite?
Leela: very. it's a system. the clerk didn't make the rules
Afreen: ok drafting now. "Dear Sir/Madam, I regret the delay in renewal..."
Leela: perfect start
Afreen: sent. got a receipt number
Leela: see. done by 4 pm

qa.q: How late was Afreen's licence renewal?
What was Afreen feeling about the municipal office?
qa.a: Afreen felt resentful and irritated, wanting to write an angry letter about their own delays.

qa.q: What did Leela advise instead of an angry letter?
qa.a: Replying honestly before the deadline, attaching the discharge paper, paying the official late fee, and being polite.

qa.q: How might the clerk at the office see Afreen's reply?
qa.a: The clerk is likely to process a polite, accurate reply smoothly, seeing it as a routine matter rather than a fight.

grounding: The protagonist resists treating a late-renewal notice as a personal attack and responds on time, honestly and politely.
